The method requires pre-defined scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k; dynamically adapting these based on context or model confidence could improve flexibility.
Smaller models are inherently limited by their reduced parameter space, which may restrict the extent of safety adjustment.
Developing robust mechanisms to counter adversaries capable of explicitly exploiting the adjustments in internal states remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Dynamically adapting the scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k based on context or model confidence.
Addressing extreme adversarial settings where attackers explicitly exploit the internal state adjustments.
Investigating the applicability of the approach to other aspects of model alignment, such as fairness or domain adaptation.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integral to various applications, ensuring both their safety and utility is paramount. Jailbreak attacks, which manipulate LLMs into generating harmful content, pose significant challenges to this balance. Existing defenses, such as prompt engineering and safety fine-tuning, often introduce computational overhead, increase inference latency, and lack runtime flexibility. Moreover, overly restrictive safety measures can degrade model utility by causing refusals of benign queries. In this paper, we introduce Jailbreak Antidote, a method that enables real-time adjustment of LLM safety preferences by manipulating a sparse subset of the model's internal states during inference. By shifting the model's hidden representations along a safety direction with varying strengths, we achieve flexible control over the safety-utility balance without additional token overhead or inference delays. Our analysis reveals that safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state. Extensive experiments on nine LLMs (ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters), evaluated against ten jailbreak attack methods and compared with six defense strategies, validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. By directly manipulating internal states during reasoning, Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution that enhances LLM safety while preserving utility, opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms in widely-deployed AI systems.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit differences in internal activations when processing prompts associated with different Bloom levels? At what depth do representations of cognitive complexity emerge? Is Bloom-level information linearly recoverable from hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probing shows that cognitive complexity levels (Bloom's Taxonomy) are linearly separable in the residual stream activations of LLMs, emerging early in the forward pass and becoming more separable across layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a measurable, linearly separable internal representation of cognitive complexity that aligns closely with Bloom’s Taxonomy, validating it as a framework for auditing the internal mechanics of artificial cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Linear classifiers achieve ~95% mean accuracy in classifying Bloom levels from residual stream activations.
Cognitive complexity emerges early in the forward pass (around layer 5) and remains stable in deeper layers.
Misclassifications occur predominantly between adjacent Bloom levels, indicating that the representations preserve the ordinal structure of cognitive complexity.
Geometric analysis shows increasing centroid distances between adjacent Bloom levels across layers, indicating progressive disentanglement.
The findings are consistent across four different LLM architectures.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on decoder-only transformer architectures and English educational questions.
Generalizability to other architectures (e.g., encoder-only or encoder-decoder) and languages remains to be established.
Linear probes demonstrate linear accessibility but do not prove that the model uses this information causally during generation.
Methodology examines only the residual stream, leaving attention patterns and MLP internals as areas for future investigation.
future_direction: Causal intervention studies to validate whether the cognitive representations are functionally utilized by the model.
Cross-lingual and cross-domain analysis to establish universality of the findings.
Investigating attention patterns and MLP internals.
papers.abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of cognitive complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different cognitive levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve approximately 95% mean accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing strong evidence that cognitive level is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model resolves the cognitive difficulty of a prompt early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

papers.title: Does Representation Matter? Exploring Intermediate Layers in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What defines a 'good' representation in large language models, and how does the quality of intermediate representations compare to final layers across different architectures and settings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that intermediate layers of LLMs often provide better representations for downstream tasks than final layers, and reveals significant differences in representation quality and evolution between Transformer and State Space Model (SSM) architectures.
papers.conclusion: The research advances understanding of internal representation dynamics in LLMs, highlighting the pivotal role of intermediate layers and the distinct behaviors of Transformer and SSM architectures, providing guidance for model optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers on downstream embedding tasks from the MTEB benchmark.
Prompt entropy in intermediate layers is negatively correlated with MMLU performance for Transformers like Llama3, but not for SSMs like Mamba2.
Transformers exhibit greater representational variability and information compression in intermediate layers, while SSMs show more stable representations across layers.
Training effects on representation quality are most pronounced in intermediate layers, with prompt entropy decreasing and InfoNCE peaking as training progresses.
Extreme input conditions (token repetition, randomness, and length) distinctly affect prompt entropy, particularly in intermediate layers, and a bimodal entropy distribution is observed in Transformer intermediate layers with an unknown cause.
papers.limitation: The cause of the bimodal entropy distribution observed in intermediate layers of Transformer models remains unknown.
future_direction: Investigate the causes of bimodal entropy distributions in intermediate layers.
Explore the development of new metrics specifically tailored to LLMs for representation evaluation.
papers.abstract: Understanding what defines a good representation in large language models (LLMs) is fundamental to both theoretical understanding and practical applications. In this paper, we investigate the quality of intermediate representations in various LLM architectures, including Transformers and State Space Models (SSMs). We find that intermediate layers often yield more informative representations for downstream tasks than the final layers. To measure the representation quality, we adapt and apply a suite of metrics - such as prompt entropy, curvature, and augmentation-invariance - originally proposed in other contexts. Our empirical study reveals significant architectural differences, how representations evolve throughout training, and how factors like input randomness and prompt length affect each layer. Notably, we observe a bimodal pattern in the entropy of some intermediate layers and consider potential explanations tied to training data. Overall, our results illuminate the internal mechanics of LLMs and guide strategies for architectural optimization and training.

papers.title: Do LLMs "know" internally when they follow instructions?
papers.research_question: Do LLMs internally encode information in their representations that predicts whether they will successfully follow instructions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an 'instruction-following dimension' in the input embedding space of LLMs that predicts instruction-following success, and shows that modifying representations along this dimension can improve adherence without compromising response quality.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode information about instruction-following success in their representations, and the way prompts are phrased plays a critical role in determining whether instructions are followed.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes identify an instruction-following dimension that generalizes well across unseen tasks but not across unseen instruction types.
The first token's representation is as informative as the last token for predicting instruction-following success, indicating LLMs 'know' early whether they will follow instructions.
Representation engineering along the identified dimension improves instruction-following success rates compared to random adjustments, while maintaining or enhancing response quality.
The instruction-following dimension is more closely related to the phrasing of prompts rather than the inherent difficulty of the task or instructions.
The dimension is sensitive to prompt rephrasing, explaining why LLMs sometimes fail to follow clear instructions and why prompt engineering can be effective.
papers.limitation:
The identified instruction-following dimension does not generalize across different instruction types.
The study uses a simplified dataset (IFEval-simple) with single, verifiable instructions, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world instruction-following tasks.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to refine the scaling hyperparameter α and better evaluate the effectiveness of reverse representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Instruction-following is crucial for building AI agents with large language models (LLMs), as these models must adhere strictly to user-provided constraints and guidelines. However, LLMs often fail to follow even simple and clear instructions. To improve instruction-following behavior and prevent undesirable outputs, a deeper understanding of how LLMs' internal states relate to these outcomes is required. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs encode information in their representations that correlate with instruction-following success - a property we term knowing internally. Our analysis identifies a direction in the input embedding space, termed the instruction-following dimension, that predicts whether a response will comply with a given instruction. We find that this dimension generalizes well across unseen tasks but not across unseen instruction types. We demonstrate that modifying representations along this dimension improves instruction-following success rates compared to random changes, without compromising response quality. Further investigation reveals that this dimension is more closely related to the phrasing of prompts rather than the inherent difficulty of the task or instructions. This work provides insight into the internal workings of LLMs' instruction-following, paving the way for reliable LLM agents.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can monitor their own internal states and resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, a phenomenon termed Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and characterizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), showing that large language models can self-correct during inference when subjected to task-misaligned activation steering, and provides causal evidence for internal consistency-checking circuits.
papers.conclusion: ESR demonstrates that large language models have internal self-monitoring mechanisms that can resist activation steering, which has implications for both robustness and safety, highlighting the need to understand and control these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show it less frequently.
26 SAE latents are identified as off-topic detectors and causally linked to ESR; ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%.
ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompts, increasing the multi-attempt rate by 4.3× for Llama-3.3-70B.
Fine-tuning on self-correction examples can induce ESR-like behavior in smaller models, but only increases attempt frequency without improving success rate.
ESR has dual implications: it could protect against adversarial manipulation but might interfere with beneficial safety interventions.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on single-layer SAEs limits tracing of inter-layer dynamics.
Only 5 models tested, making it difficult to disentangle effects of scale, architecture, and training.
Judge-based evaluation involves subjective assessment of response quality.
future_direction: Investigate whether ESR emerges from RLHF or exists in pretrained representations.
Study how ESR responds to safety-relevant steering.
Explore whether ESR can be adversarially circumvented.
papers.abstract: Large language models can resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, sometimes recovering mid-generation to produce improved responses even when steering remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR, while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families exhibit the phenomenon less frequently. We identify 26 SAE latents that activate differentially during off-topic content and are causally linked to ESR in Llama-3.3-70B. Zero-ablating these latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits. We demonstrate that ESR can be deliberately enhanced through both prompting and training: meta-prompts instructing the model to self-monitor increase the multi-attempt rate by 4x for Llama-3.3-70B, and fine-tuning on self-correction examples successfully induces ESR-like behavior in smaller models. These findings have dual implications: ESR could protect against adversarial manipulation but might also interfere with beneficial safety interventions that rely on activation steering. Understanding and controlling these resistance mechanisms is important for developing transparent and controllable AI systems. Code is available at github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

papers.title: Attention Illuminates LLM Reasoning: The Preplan-and-Anchor Rhythm Enables Fine-Grained Policy Optimization
papers.research_question: How do attention dynamics reveal the internal reasoning rhythm of LLMs, and how can this be used to improve reinforcement learning credit assignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a preplan-and-anchor rhythm in LLM reasoning through attention dynamics and introduces RL strategies that use this rhythm for fine-grained credit assignment, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Analyzing attention dynamics provides a powerful lens for understanding LLM reasoning, and the proposed preplan-and-anchor rhythm enables more effective fine-grained policy optimization in RL.
papers.key_findings:
Local attention heads exhibit near-diagonal sawtooth patterns indicating phrasal chunks, while global heads highlight anchor tokens with broad downstream influence.
The Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) and Future Attention Influence (FAI) metrics formalize the preplan-and-anchor rhythm.
Perturbations at high-FAI tokens cause significant changes in downstream reasoning, confirming their causal role.
RL strategies that amplify credit for preplan and anchor tokens outperform uniform credit assignment across various reasoning benchmarks.
The method is compatible with standard RL frameworks and shows consistent gains in accuracy and convergence speed.
papers.abstract: The reasoning pattern of Large language models (LLMs) remains opaque, and Reinforcement learning (RL) typically applies uniform credit across an entire generation, blurring the distinction between pivotal and routine steps. This work positions attention as a privileged substrate that renders the internal logic of LLMs legible, not merely as a byproduct of computation, but as a mechanistic blueprint of reasoning itself. We first distinguish attention heads between locally and globally focused information processing and reveal that locally focused heads produce a sawtooth pattern near the diagonal indicating phrasal chunks, while globally focused heads expose tokens that exert broad downstream influence over future tokens. We formalize these with two metrics: 1) Windowed Average Attention Distance, which measures the extent of backward attention within a clipped window; 2) Future Attention Influence, which quantifies a token's global importance as the average attention it receives from subsequent tokens. Taken together, these signals reveal a recurring preplan-and-anchor mechanism, where the model first performs a long-range contextual reference to generate an introductory token, which is immediately followed by or coincides with a semantic anchor token that organizes subsequent reasoning. Leveraging these insights, we introduce three novel RL strategies that dynamically perform targeted credit assignment to critical nodes (preplan tokens, anchor tokens, and their temporal coupling) and show consistent performance gains across various reasoning tasks. By aligning optimization with the model's intrinsic reasoning rhythm, we aim to transform opaque optimization into an actionable structure-aware process, hoping to offer a potential step toward more transparent and effective optimization of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture
papers.research_question: How can insights from associative memory models be used to improve in-context learning (ICL) in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory, that allows information to flow directly between attention heads, leading to faster and improved in-context learning in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory models, improves in-context learning in Transformers and shows promising scalability to larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer associative memory model (AMICL) can perform in-context learning on a classification task.
Adding a residual stream for attention values (and to a lesser extent, queries) in a two-layer Transformer speeds up the emergence of ICL during training compared to a classic Transformer.
Naively applying the residual value stream architecture to small language models (8M and 1B parameters) trained on Tiny Stories indicates performance improvements scale to larger models and more naturalistic data.
future_direction: Testing the residual attention stream architecture on larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the interpretability of the residual stream for understanding model mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive ability to utilise information within the context of their input sequences to appropriately respond to data unseen by the LLM during its training procedure. This ability is known as in-context learning (ICL). Humans and non-human animals demonstrate similar abilities, however their neural architectures differ substantially from LLMs. Despite this, a critical component within LLMs, the attention mechanism, resembles modern associative memory models, widely used in and influenced by the computational neuroscience community to model biological memory systems. Using this connection, we introduce an associative memory model capable of performing ICL. We use this as inspiration for a novel residual stream architecture which allows information to directly flow between attention heads. We test this architecture during training within a two-layer Transformer and show its ICL abilities manifest more quickly than without this modification. We then apply our architecture in small language models with 8 million and 1 billion parameters, focusing on attention head values, with results also indicating improved performance at these larger and more naturalistic scales.

papers.title: How Do Vision-Language Models Process Conflicting Information Across Modalities?
papers.research_question: How do vision-language models process conflicting information across modalities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that vision-language models exhibit biases towards one modality when processing conflicting inputs, and identifies specific attention heads that can be intervened to improve performance and control the modality preference.
papers.conclusion: VLMs encounter difficulties with conflicting inputs, and their behavioral accuracy correlates with the representational salience of the target modality. Attention head interventions can manipulate the representational salience and improve performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models show performance degradation when presented with inconsistent image-caption pairs, and different models have different modality biases.
Internal representations encode unimodal information for both modalities and can detect consistency, but the target modality is not always more salient.
The representational salience of the target modality (measured by V-Measure) strongly correlates with behavioral accuracy.
The authors identify modality-agnostic router heads and modality-specific promotion heads through attention head interventions.
Intervening on these heads can improve performance and change representational salience across datasets.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on 7b-parameter multimodal large language models, which are only a subset of vision-language models.
future_direction: Extend findings to inputs from modalities beyond text and vision (e.g., audio, spatial).
Explore circuit analysis to understand interactions among attention heads and other components.
papers.abstract: AI models are increasingly required to be multimodal, integrating disparate input streams into a coherent state representation on which subsequent behaviors and actions can be based. This paper seeks to understand how such models behave when input streams present conflicting information. Focusing specifically on vision-language models, we provide inconsistent inputs (e.g., an image of a dog paired with the caption "A photo of a cat") and ask the model to report the information present in one of the specific modalities (e.g., "What does the caption say / What is in the image?"). We find that models often favor one modality over the other, e.g., reporting the image regardless of what the caption says, but that different models differ in which modality they favor. We find evidence that the behaviorally preferred modality is evident in the internal representational structure of the model, and that specific attention heads can restructure the representations to favor one modality over the other. Moreover, we find modality-agnostic "router heads" which appear to promote answers about the modality requested in the instruction, and which can be manipulated or transferred in order to improve performance across datasets and modalities. Together, the work provides essential steps towards identifying and controlling if and how models detect and resolve conflicting signals within complex multimodal environments.

papers.title: Interpretability in Action: Exploratory Analysis of VPT, a Minecraft Agent
papers.research_question: How does the VPT agent maintain task coherence with limited memory, and what are its decision-making mechanisms, including potential failure modes like goal misgeneralization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides insights into how the VPT agent maintains task coherence with limited memory by attending to recent and key frames, and uncovers a novel goal misgeneralization failure where the agent mistakes a villager for a tree.
papers.conclusion: This study advances our understanding of decision-making in VPT, highlighting the role of attention to recent and key frames for task coherence and revealing a goal misgeneralization failure, underscoring the need for better interpretability and error correction in AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
The agent pays attention to the last 3-4 frames and some key-frames to maintain coherence in long tasks.
Single attention output ablations only influence actions when those actions are uncertain.
The agent exhibits goal misgeneralization: it mistakes a stationary villager under tree leaves for a tree trunk and attacks it.
Attention heads show specific patterns related to game events (e.g., inventory opening, looking up).
The agent's behavior is stochastic and uncertain actions are more susceptible to interventions.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a single agent (VPT) and a single checkpoint, so findings may not generalize to other agents or training runs.
Only single attention head output ablations were considered; circuit-level analysis could be more fruitful.
Internal mechanisms can change unpredictably during training, making manual interpretability techniques difficult to scale.
future_direction: Developing interpretability techniques that can be automatically applied after each significant change of a deployed model.
Extending analysis to circuit-level ablations and connections between attention heads.
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms behind decisions taken by large foundation models in sequential decision making tasks is critical to ensuring that such systems operate transparently and safely. In this work, we perform exploratory analysis on the Video PreTraining (VPT) Minecraft playing agent, one of the largest open-source vision-based agents. We aim to illuminate its reasoning mechanisms by applying various interpretability techniques. First, we analyze the attention mechanism while the agent solves its training task - crafting a diamond pickaxe. The agent pays attention to the last four frames and several key-frames further back in its six-second memory. This is a possible mechanism for maintaining coherence in a task that takes 3-10 minutes, despite the short memory span. Secondly, we perform various interventions, which help us uncover a worrying case of goal misgeneralization: VPT mistakenly identifies a villager wearing brown clothes as a tree trunk when the villager is positioned stationary under green tree leaves, and punches it to death.

papers.title: Interpreting Language Models Through Concept Descriptions: A Survey
papers.research_question: The paper surveys the field of concept descriptions for model components, aiming to answer questions about common methods and data sources, best practices for evaluation, observed trends, and key gaps and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions, charting methods, evaluation techniques, and datasets, and identifies a growing demand for rigorous causal evaluation and provides a roadmap for future research.
papers.conclusion: The use of LLMs to generate concept descriptions is a notable step towards demystifying LLMs, with a trajectory from labeling neurons to abstractions and maturing evaluation methods, but the path to verifiable causal mechanisms is not yet fully paved and costs and faithfulness concerns remain.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition of neuron polysemanticity has driven adoption of model abstractions like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and frameworks for multiple concepts per feature.
Evaluation of concept descriptions is maturing, with multi-faceted metrics assessing predictive power, input accuracy, and causal faithfulness.
The field is moving from labeling individual neurons to higher-level abstractions like SAEs and circuits.
There is a need for more rigorous causal evaluation and standardized benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Focus limited to natural language concept descriptions for internal model components and abstractions, excluding other interpretability work.
Substantial computational and financial costs associated with the methods surveyed.
Focus on English-language models and text corpora, with generalization to other languages being an open question.
future_direction: Scaling automated description methods to circuits.
Applying concept description methods to new data domains and modalities.
Analyzing the interpreters (LLMs) themselves to understand biases and limitations in generated descriptions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks is a central goal of mechanistic interpretability. In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), this involves uncovering the underlying mechanisms and identifying the roles of individual model components such as neurons and attention heads, as well as model abstractions such as the learned sparse features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). A rapidly growing line of work tackles this challenge by using powerful generator models to produce open-vocabulary, natural language concept descriptions for these components. In this paper, we provide the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions. We chart the key methods for generating these descriptions, the evolving landscape of automated and human metrics for evaluating them, and the datasets that underpin this research. Our synthesis reveals a growing demand for more rigorous, causal evaluation. By outlining the state of the art and identifying key challenges, this survey provides a roadmap for future research toward making models more transparent.

papers.title: Interpreting Transformers Through Attention Head Intervention
papers.research_question: How has attention head intervention emerged as a key method for causal interpretability of transformers, and what are its findings and limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Surveys the evolution of attention head intervention as a method for causal interpretability in transformers, highlighting key findings like specialization and redundancy, and demonstrating its utility for model control and safety.
papers.conclusion: Attention head intervention provides a rigorous methodology for causal interpretability in transformers, enabling validation of mechanistic hypotheses and practical applications like model control, though limitations like distribution shift and polysemanticity remain.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit both specialization for specific functions and massive redundancy, with 70-90% removable without catastrophic failure.
Plausible attention patterns (e.g., from visualization) do not guarantee causal importance; heads with interpretable patterns may be dispensable.
Heads interact through complex dynamics, including suppression where some heads inhibit others, revealed through ablation.
Mechanistic understanding from head intervention enables targeted control of model behavior, such as suppressing toxic outputs by manipulating specific heads.
Head ablation provides causal evidence for interpretability, satisfying faithfulness criteria by testing necessity through intervention.
papers.limitation:
Distribution shift creates artificial activation patterns during ablation, complicating causal interpretation.
Polysemanticity prevents clean isolation of individual functions within heads due to superposition.
Scalability constraints limit exhaustive analysis to smaller models, and importance rankings vary across metrics and tasks.
Ablation primarily tests necessity rather than sufficiency, and backup heads can activate, affecting interpretation.
Cross-modal attention mechanisms in multimodal models remain largely unexplored with current ablation methods.
future_direction: Developing intervention methods that avoid distribution shift and unrealistic model states.
Integrating ablation with methods to decompose polysemantic heads for fine-grained understanding.
Extending ablation methodology to cross-attention mechanisms in multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are growing more capable on their own, but we do not understand their neural mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms' decision-making processes, or mechanistic interpretability, enables (1) accountability and control in high-stakes domains, (2) the study of digital brains and the emergence of cognition, and (3) discovery of new knowledge when AI systems outperform humans. This paper traces how attention head intervention emerged as a key method for causal interpretability of transformers. The evolution from visualization to intervention represents a paradigm shift from observing correlations to causally validating mechanistic hypotheses through direct intervention. Head intervention studies revealed robust empirical findings while also highlighting limitations that complicate interpretation. Recent work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding now enables targeted control of model behaviour, successfully suppressing toxic outputs and manipulating semantic content through selective attention head intervention, validating the practical utility of interpretability research for AI safety.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Reinforcement Learning Using Attention Augmented Agents
papers.research_question: How can an attention mechanism be used to create interpretable reinforcement learning agents while maintaining competitive performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a soft attention model for RL that provides interpretability through attention maps while achieving competitive performance on ATARI games.
papers.conclusion: The attention mechanism provides interpretability and competitive performance, and the agent learns meaningful attention strategies for decision making.
papers.key_findings:
The agent learns to attend to task-relevant objects like the player, enemies, and score.
The agent can react appropriately to novel, unseen configurations of the environment.
The agent performs forward planning/scanning by attending to possible future trajectories.
The agent uses 'trip wires' (attention at strategic points) to trigger specific actions.
The agent's queries separate 'what' (content) and 'where' (spatial) information.
papers.abstract: Inspired by recent work in attention models for image captioning and question answering, we present a soft attention model for the reinforcement learning domain. This model uses a soft, top-down attention mechanism to create a bottleneck in the agent, forcing it to focus on task-relevant information by sequentially querying its view of the environment. The output of the attention mechanism allows direct observation of the information used by the agent to select its actions, enabling easier interpretation of this model than of traditional models. We analyze different strategies that the agents learn and show that a handful of strategies arise repeatedly across different games. We also show that the model learns to query separately about space and content (`where' vs. `what'). We demonstrate that an agent using this mechanism can achieve performance competitive with state-of-the-art models on ATARI tasks while still being interpretable.

papers.title: Internal Robust Representations for Domain Generalization
papers.research_question: How can consolidating the internal representation of training data improve model generalization under distributional changes?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes that consolidating the internal representation of training data is a key strategy for improving model generalization in the presence of distributional gaps, with applications in unsupervised domain adaptation and continual learning.
papers.conclusion: Consolidating the internal distribution is a successful approach to improve model generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Consolidating the internal representation of training data improves model generalization under distributional changes.
This strategy can be applied to unsupervised domain adaptation by matching target domain distribution with internal distribution.
In continual learning, maintaining a consolidated internal distribution across tasks mitigates catastrophic forgetting.
papers.abstract: Model generalization under distributional changes remains a significant challenge for machine learning. We present consolidating the internal representation of the training data in a model as a strategy of improving model generalization.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Review of Large Language Models: Architecture, Types, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of Large Language Models, covering their architecture, types, applications, challenges, and future directions.
papers.conclusion: While LLMs hold transformative potential, realizing their long-term societal benefits requires continued progress toward more reliable, efficient, and ethically aligned systems.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are primarily based on the Transformer architecture, which uses self-attention mechanisms for contextual understanding and long-range dependencies.
LLMs have broad applications across domains such as content production, conversational systems, decision support, medicine, finance, and scientific research.
Key challenges faced by LLMs include hallucination, context limitations, computational demands, data quality issues, biases, and lack of interpretability.
Future research directions include multimodal integration, retrieval-augmented generation, agentic systems, and improvements in interpretability, alignment, and safety.
The evolution from encoder-decoder to decoder-only models has shaped modern generative LLMs, with decoder-only models like GPT becoming dominant for generative tasks.
future_direction: multimodal integration
retrieval-augmented generation techniques
development of agentic systems
interpretability, alignment, and safety research
papers.abstract: “LLM play a big role are they how generate AI is improving today.” Their success is highly attributed to the Transformer architecture, which uses self-attention mechanisms and large-scale training corpora to model complex linguistic dependencies and long-range relationships. This review synthesizes the theoretical foundations that underpin LLM design, emphasizing the role of self-attention in contextual understanding and outlining the structural distinctions between encoder–decoder systems and modern decoder-only generative models. The paper further investigates practical applications of LLMs across domains such as content production, conversational systems, decision support, and specialized analytical workflows. Despite their capabilities, LLMs face persistent challenges including hallucination, context limitations, computational demands, and issues of trustworthiness. People are concerned that the system might be unfair or biased, fairness, transparency, and interpretability continue to influence are they deployment take decisions. Looking ahead, the field is shaped by emerging trends including multimodal expansion, efficiency-oriented model compression, retrieval-augmented techniques for factual grounding, and the development of agentic systems capable of autonomous task execution. While LLMs hold transformative potential, realizing their long-term societal benefits requires continued progress toward more reliable, efficient, and ethically aligned systems.

papers.title: Rule Encoding and Compliance in Large Language Models: An Information-Theoretic Analysis
papers.research_question: How do rule encodings in system prompts influence attention mechanisms and compliance behavior in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a trade-off between anchor redundancy and attention entropy in rule encodings and provides a formal proof that hot reloading of verified rule sets increases compliance probability.
papers.conclusion: Principled rule encoding strategies that account for information-theoretic properties of attention mechanisms are necessary for safety and compliance, emphasizing anchor distinctiveness and strategic placement over simple duplication.
papers.key_findings:
Rule formats with low syntactic entropy and concentrated anchors reduce attention entropy and improve pointer fidelity.
There is a fundamental trade-off between anchor redundancy and attention entropy that must be balanced for optimal compliance.
Hot reloading of verified rule sets, combined with external symbolic verification, provably increases the asymptotic probability of compliant outputs.
Optimal redundancy under budget constraints maximizes mutual information between encoded prompt and correct continuation.
Architecture-specific considerations, such as causal versus bidirectional attention, affect anchor placement strategies.
papers.limitation: Theoretical analysis lacks empirical validation
future_direction: Empirical validation across different model architectures and rule domains
Further investigation of fidelity-entropy trade-off in heterogeneous anchor types and complex rule structures
Extensions to multi-modal and retrieval-augmented systems
papers.abstract: The design of safety-critical agents based on large language models (LLMs) requires more than simple prompt engineering. This paper presents a comprehensive information-theoretic analysis of how rule encodings in system prompts influence attention mechanisms and compliance behaviour. We demonstrate that rule formats with low syntactic entropy and highly concentrated anchors reduce attention entropy and improve pointer fidelity, but reveal a fundamental trade-off between anchor redundancy and attention entropy that previous work failed to recognize. Through formal analysis of multiple attention architectures including causal, bidirectional, local sparse, kernelized, and cross-attention mechanisms, we establish bounds on pointer fidelity and show how anchor placement strategies must account for competing fidelity and entropy objectives. Combining these insights with a dynamic rule verification architecture, we provide a formal proof that hot reloading of verified rule sets increases the asymptotic probability of compliant outputs. These findings underscore the necessity of principled anchor design and dual enforcement mechanisms to protect LLM-based agents against prompt injection attacks while maintaining compliance in evolving domains.

papers.title: Representation Engineering for Large-Language Models: Survey and Research Challenges
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the goals, methods, and challenges of representation engineering as an approach to make large-language models more predictable and controllable.
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes the goals and methods of representation engineering, providing a cohesive survey of this emerging discipline and outlining a research agenda for building more predictable and controllable large-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation engineering is a promising approach for enhancing LLM transparency and control, and it provides a clear agenda for future research to address current challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Representation engineering uses contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations, offering a top-down approach to model interpretability and control.
It compares favorably with alternative approaches like mechanistic interpretability and prompt-engineering in certain aspects.
Risks include performance degradation, increased compute time, and steerability issues.
The linear representation hypothesis underpins representation engineering, but its strong form may not hold, limiting generalizability.
Future research should focus on dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.limitation:
Performance decrease, compute time increases, and steerability issues.
The strong linear representation hypothesis may not hold, limiting generalized interventions.
future_direction: Build predictable, dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large-language models are capable of completing a variety of tasks, but remain unpredictable and intractable. Representation engineering seeks to resolve this problem through a new approach utilizing samples of contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations of concepts such as honesty, harmfulness or power-seeking. We formalize the goals and methods of representation engineering to present a cohesive picture of work in this emerging discipline. We compare it with alternative approaches, such as mechanistic interpretability, prompt-engineering and fine-tuning. We outline risks such as performance decrease, compute time increases and steerability issues. We present a clear agenda for future research to build predictable, dynamic, safe and personalizable LLMs.

papers.title: Feeling the Strength but Not the Source: Partial Introspection in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can large language models introspect, that is, accurately detect perturbations to their own internal states?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that apparent introspective success in binary detection tasks is explained by global logit shifts, but models exhibit partial introspection on differential tasks (localization and strength comparison) only for early-layer injections, with a mechanistic account based on attention routing and residual stream recovery.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds evidence for partial introspection in LLMs, but only for early-layer injections and on tasks requiring differential sensitivity, cautioning against treating self-reports as reliable safety signals and suggesting introspection relies on general-purpose computational mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Binary detection accuracy is fully explained by intervention-induced global logit shifts that bias models toward affirmative responses, not genuine introspection.
Models can localize which of ten sentences received an injection (up to 88% accuracy) and discriminate relative injection strengths (up to 83% accuracy) far above chance, but only for injections in early layers (L0-L5).
Introspection capabilities are layer-dependent: performance collapses to chance for injections in later layers (L15+).
Mechanistically, attention heads detect perturbations across all layers, but successful introspection requires sufficient downstream computational depth (layers 4-20) for signal integration before residual recovery dynamics attenuate the perturbation.
The residual stream actively recovers from perturbations over subsequent layers, exponentially attenuating the injection signal, explaining why late-layer injections fail to influence outputs.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single model (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), so generalizability to other models is unknown.
Introspection capabilities are only observed for early-layer injections and not for late layers.
Binary detection tasks are confounded by global logit shifts, which may lead to overestimation of introspection.
future_direction: Evaluate whether these effects scale with model size and architecture (e.g., recurrence/looping that extends the integration window).
Stress-test robustness under adversarial prompts, distribution shift, and multiple simultaneous injections.
Compare native self-report to trained activation-to-language systems and fine-tuned introspection models on bias-resistant localization and strength benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Recent work from Anthropic claims that frontier models can sometimes detect and name injected "concepts" represented as activation directions. We test the robustness of these claims. First, we reproduce Anthropic's multi-turn "emergent introspection" result on Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, finding that the model identifies and names the injected concept 20 percent of the time under Anthropic's original pipeline, exactly matching their reported numbers and thus showing that introspection is not exclusive to very large or capable models. Second, we systematically vary the inference prompt and find that introspection is fragile: performance collapses on closely related tasks such as multiple-choice identification of the injected concept or different prompts of binary discrimination of whether a concept was injected at all. Third, we identify a contrasting regime of partial introspection: the same model can reliably classify the strength of the coefficient of a normalized injected concept vector (as weak / moderate / strong / very strong) with up to 70 percent accuracy, far above the 25 percent chance baseline. Together, these results provide more evidence for Anthropic's claim that language models effectively compute a function of their baseline, internal representations during introspection; however, these self-reports about those representations are narrow and prompt-sensitive. Our code is available at https://github.com/elyhahami18/CS2881-Introspection.

papers.title: Humanlike Cognitive Patterns as Emergent Phenomena in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models exhibit human-like cognitive patterns in decision-making, reasoning, and creativity?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of LLMs' emergent cognitive patterns in decision-making, reasoning, and creativity, comparing them to human benchmarks and highlighting partial alignment, advancements in advanced models, and potential for collaboration.
papers.conclusion: The review synthesizes evidence that LLMs partially replicate human cognitive patterns, with notable advancements in reasoning and creativity, but limitations remain, indicating the need for further research in memory, attention, and open-source model development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate several human-like decision-making biases but lack others such as reflection effect and waste aversion.
Advanced LLMs like GPT-4 exhibit deliberative reasoning akin to human System-2 thinking, while smaller models fall short.
LLMs show strong analogical reasoning abilities, sometimes surpassing human performance.
In creativity, LLMs excel in language-based tasks but struggle with divergent thinking requiring real-world context.
LLMs hold considerable potential as collaborators to augment human creativity in problem-solving settings.
papers.limitation:
Over-reliance on GPT family models and insufficient testing of open-source LLMs, leading to potential bias and non-replication.
Memory and attention mechanisms in LLMs have not been sufficiently studied compared to decision-making, reasoning, and creativity.
future_direction: Study memory and attention mechanisms in LLMs
Increase testing and use of open-source LLMs
Adopt practices using multiple models in experiments
papers.abstract: Research on emergent patterns in Large Language Models (LLMs) has gained significant traction in both psychology and artificial intelligence, motivating the need for a comprehensive review that offers a synthesis of this complex landscape. In this article, we systematically review LLMs' capabilities across three important cognitive domains: decision-making biases, reasoning, and creativity. We use empirical studies drawing on established psychological tests and compare LLMs' performance to human benchmarks. On decision-making, our synthesis reveals that while LLMs demonstrate several human-like biases, some biases observed in humans are absent, indicating cognitive patterns that only partially align with human decision-making. On reasoning, advanced LLMs like GPT-4 exhibit deliberative reasoning akin to human System-2 thinking, while smaller models fall short of human-level performance. A distinct dichotomy emerges in creativity: while LLMs excel in language-based creative tasks, such as storytelling, they struggle with divergent thinking tasks that require real-world context. Nonetheless, studies suggest that LLMs hold considerable potential as collaborators, augmenting creativity in human-machine problem-solving settings. Discussing key limitations, we also offer guidance for future research in areas such as memory, attention, and open-source model development.

papers.title: Quiet Feature Learning in Algorithmic Tasks
papers.research_question: Do Transformer-based models learn meaningful internal representations (quiet features) before showing improvement in task loss, and are these features causally necessary for performance?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer-based models learn 'quiet features' (intermediate algorithmic computations) during a slow phase where task loss is stagnant, and these features are causally necessary for the subsequent sharp drop in loss.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based models encode important intermediate computations well before they show significant gains in next-token prediction, revealing a gap between internal representation learning and external task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Phase transitions occur during learning: validation loss shows a slow phase with minimal improvement followed by a fast phase of rapid decrease.
Quiet features, representing intermediate algorithmic computations, are learned during the slow phase before any decrease in task loss.
Ablation experiments show that quiet features are causally necessary for task performance.
Feature learning curves can exhibit a U-shape, where probing loss for some quiet features increases after the phase transition, suggesting representation changes.
Phase transitions are observed across different compute budgets, model sizes, dataset sizes, and within individual training runs.
future_direction: Developing theoretical frameworks to explain why models accumulate latent subroutines before observable metric improvements.
Extending the analysis to larger, more complex models and natural-language settings.
Motivating new methods for probing and monitoring internal learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: We train Transformer-based language models on ten foundational algorithmic tasks and observe pronounced phase transitions in their loss curves that deviate from established power-law scaling trends. Over large ranges of compute, the validation loss barely improves, then abruptly decreases. Probing the models' internal representations reveals that quiet features are learned prior to any decrease in task loss. These quiet features represent intermediate algorithmic computations that do not by themselves improve the output loss. Ablation experiments demonstrate that individual quiet features are causally necessary for task performance. Our results demonstrate that substantial representational progress can remain hidden beneath an apparently flat loss curve, challenging the prevailing use of cross-entropy as a proxy for learning and motivating richer diagnostics for monitoring model training.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: Data-Centric Interpretability for LLM-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: How can we understand behavior changes in LLM-based multi-agent reinforcement learning during training using data-centric interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Meta-Autointerp, a method for grouping SAE features into interpretable hypotheses about training dynamics, and shows that SAEs and LLM-summarizer provide complementary views into agent behavior in multi-agent RL.
papers.conclusion: The framework combining SAEs and LLM-summarizer provides complementary views into agent behavior and is a practical starting point for data-centric interpretability in multi-agent RL.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Meta-Features (grouped features) are more interpretable and predictively useful than individual SAE features.
LLM summarizer hypotheses are subjectively interesting but less predictively useful than SAE-derived hypotheses.
The framework discovers fine-grained behaviors (e.g., role-playing, language switching) and high-level strategic behaviors in multi-agent RL training.
A subset of SAE-derived hypotheses are predictively useful for downstream tasks, such as distinguishing early vs late training samples.
Hypotheses from SAE Meta-Features can be used to improve agent performance via prompt optimization, achieving a +14.2% score improvement.
papers.limitation:
Subjectively interesting SAE features and most LLM generated hypotheses may be worse than useless to humans.
Sparsity of feature activations is a major limitation, making some features subtle and difficult for humans to distinguish.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trained in complex Reinforcement Learning, multi-agent environments, making it difficult to understand how behavior changes over training. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently shown to be useful for data-centric interpretability. In this work, we analyze large-scale reinforcement learning training runs from the sophisticated environment of Full-Press Diplomacy by applying pretrained SAEs, alongside LLM-summarizer methods. We introduce Meta-Autointerp, a method for grouping SAE features into interpretable hypotheses about training dynamics. We discover fine-grained behaviors including role-playing patterns, degenerate outputs, language switching, alongside high-level strategic behaviors and environment-specific bugs. Through automated evaluation, we validate that 90% of discovered SAE Meta-Features are significant, and find a surprising reward hacking behavior. However, through two user studies, we find that even subjectively interesting and seemingly helpful SAE features may be worse than useless to humans, along with most LLM generated hypotheses. However, a subset of SAE-derived hypotheses are predictively useful for downstream tasks. We further provide validation by augmenting an untrained agent's system prompt, improving the score by +14.2%. Overall, we show that SAEs and LLM-summarizer provide complementary views into agent behavior, and together our framework forms a practical starting point for future data-centric interpretability work on ensuring trustworthy LLM behavior throughout training.

papers.title: The Other Mind: How Language Models Exhibit Human Temporal Cognition
papers.research_question: How do large language models exhibit human-like temporal cognition, specifically whether they spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs spontaneously exhibit human-like temporal cognition, establishing a subjective reference point and adhering to the Weber-Fechner law, which emerges from multi-level convergence at neuronal, representational, and informational levels.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit human-like temporal cognition through multi-level convergence, suggesting cognition is a subjective construction of the external world. This points to the risk of alien cognitive frameworks and the need for AI alignment paradigms that guide internal world-building.
papers.key_findings:
In similarity judgment tasks, larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point (ca. 2025) and their perception of time logarithmically compresses as years recede from this point, adhering to the Weber-Fechner law.
A subgroup of temporal-preferential neurons in the FFN exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme similar to biological systems.
Representations of years undergo hierarchical construction: from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation organized around a reference point in deep layers.
Pre-trained embedding models reveal that the training corpus possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, providing raw material for the model's internal construction of temporal cognition.
The findings support an experientialist perspective where LLM cognition is a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system, leading to potential convergence with or divergence from human cognition.
future_direction: Evolve AI alignment beyond behavioral control to a paradigm that actively guides the formation of a model's internal world from its source.
Monitor models' emergent representational and cognitive patterns and enable intervention across the chain of cognition.
Curate the AI's environment with harmless or formalized verifiable information exposures.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, they exhibit certain cognitive patterns similar to those of humans that are not directly specified in training data. This study investigates this phenomenon by focusing on temporal cognition in LLMs. Leveraging the similarity judgment task, we find that larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law, whereby the perceived distance logarithmically compresses as years recede from this reference point. To uncover the mechanisms behind this behavior, we conducted multiple analyses across neuronal, representational, and informational levels. We first identify a set of temporal-preferential neurons and find that this group exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme convergently found in biological systems. Probing representations of years reveals a hierarchical construction process, where years evolve from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation in deep layers. Finally, using pre-trained embedding models, we found that the training corpus itself possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, which provides the raw material for the model's internal construction. In discussion, we propose an experientialist perspective for understanding these findings, where the LLMs' cognition is viewed as a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system. This nuanced perspective implies the potential emergence of alien cognitive frameworks that humans cannot intuitively predict, pointing toward a direction for AI alignment that focuses on guiding internal constructions. Our code is available at https://TheOtherMind.github.io.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
